issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to justify as a salient trigger unless the disaster specifically involved a vehicle context, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other triggers ('feeling physically unwell', 'unpredictable situations') and the negative appraisals describe generalized vulnerability and loss of control, but 'similar cars' introduces a highly specific cue that does not cohere with the rest of the formulation or trauma type.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'Alcohol smell' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless supported by memory or threat content linking alcohol odor to the disaster context. Here there are no Memory or Threat items providing that connection, making this trigger clinically incoherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The formulation shows a strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals link, but the selected trigger items mostly imply internal-state or unpredictability cues, whereas 'I have to be on guard all the time' implies an ongoing external danger/threat style response. With Threat node absent and no trigger content clearly tied to vigilance for danger, this appraisal is weakly matched to the trigger pattern and stands out as formulation-incongruent in this profile.

vignette:
Minh had been working late one humid evening in his apartment tower in Seattle when the fire alarm began to pulse and the building lights flickered out. At first he assumed it was a routine drill, but within minutes the hallway outside his door filled with the sharp, bitter smell of smoke, and the announcement over the intercom became choppy with static. By the time he reached the stairwell, he could hear people shouting several floors below and feel the crush of uncertainty around him: no one could say where the smoke was coming from, whether it was contained, or which route was safest. What stayed with him most from that night was not only the smell but the bodily sensation of not feeling right in his own skin-his stomach turning, his head light, his legs unsteady as if he might faint. In the weeks afterward, those moments of feeling physically unwell and those sudden, unpredictable shifts in his surroundings became tightly linked in his mind with the thought that he had failed at the most basic task of keeping himself safe.

Before the fire, Minh had been proud of being careful, steady, and composed. He worked as a policy analyst, a job that depended on weighing contingencies and anticipating what could go wrong, and for most of his adult life that attentiveness had felt like a strength. Afterward, it became something much more frightening. When he felt even slightly ill-an uneasy stomach before breakfast, a brief wave of dizziness in a meeting, the kind of fatigue that used to mean nothing-he would become convinced that he could no longer trust himself to judge danger correctly. If his body could betray him without warning, he reasoned, then so could his mind. He had come to believe that his reactions since the event meant that he was going crazy, especially when the fear rose quickly and made his thoughts race in circles. He started checking the office exits whenever the building made an odd sound and scanning his surroundings for signs of trouble, telling himself that he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. That vigilance felt protective to him, but it also confirmed, each time he did it, how unsafe the world now seemed.

The smell of smoke was the most immediate way the memory returned. If a neighbor's barbecue drifted through the apartment courtyard, or if a passing car left a hot exhaust smell near the parking garage, Minh would feel his chest tighten before he had fully identified the source. In those moments he became certain that his body's alarm was accurate and that he could not rely on himself to stay calm or to make a good decision if another emergency came. He began to mistrust his own reactions in ordinary situations, especially when something felt off but he could not explain why, and that mistrust made him more alert to every faint scent, every flicker of uncertainty. At work, where he spent his days in a quiet government office reviewing reports and drafting recommendations, he started avoiding the conference room closest to the kitchen because burnt toast from the break area could send him back to the stairwell. He would open windows in the middle of winter and excuse himself from meetings if someone mentioned an evacuation plan, a wildfire update, or anything that hinted at unpredictability.

Over time, his life narrowed around these fears. He no longer lingered after work to talk with colleagues, and he had begun asking his wife to handle more of the errands that involved crowded places or unfamiliar routes. He disliked how often he had to apologize for leaving early or seeming distracted, but he was more afraid of what might happen if he ignored the warnings his mind kept sending. The more he watched for signs of danger, the more often he noticed his own racing pulse, queasy stomach, and brief spells of dizziness, and each episode seemed to prove that he was not the man he had been before the fire. The fear of unpredictability did not stay abstract; it followed him into elevators that jerked between floors, into weather alerts on his phone, even into the simple experience of feeling tired after lunch. What had begun as a response to one night in a smoke-filled building had become, in his experience, evidence that he must remain on guard at all times, because a moment of inattention could mean he would freeze, panic, or make some disastrous mistake.

By the time he sought help, Minh was exhausted by the effort of staying careful. He came after a week in which a faint burning smell from a delivery truck in the office parking lot sent him home early, ashamed and shaken, and he realized he was no longer sure how to tell the difference between actual danger and his own body's warnings. He wanted to believe he could trust himself again, but what frightened him most was the possibility that the next surge of fear would confirm his worst thought-that something in him had broken, and that one more unpredictable moment could send him spiraling further.
